title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E420 Euler treats the calculus of variations by embedding the extremal y(x) in a one-parameter family y(x,t), the 'method of variations'. The variation of the functional is then an ordinary t-derivative times dt. The functional is J = ∫ Z dx with Z = Z(x, y, p, q, r, s, ...), where p = y', q = y'', and so on. Euler writes dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + ... In §14 he integrated by parts and split dt·∂J/∂t into pieces. §37 (previous page) took the first piece, dt ∫ dx (∂y/∂t)(N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + d⁴S/dx⁴ − ...), integrated from A to M. Here Yυ = dt ∂y/∂t is the vertical displacement δy of the varied curve at abscissa x.

§38 (this page): Because the displacements δy inside (A, M) are arbitrary, and can change sign, this first part can take any value. The one exception is when the curve satisfies N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − ... = 0. This is the Euler–Poisson equation, the Euler–Lagrange equation for higher-order Lagrangians. Then the interior part vanishes for every neighbouring curve, so interior deviation contributes nothing. Euler concludes that on this curve ∫Z dx attains a maximum or minimum.

§39: The second part is the boundary term dt(∂y/∂t)(P − Q' + R'' − S''' + ...). Evaluated at the endpoint M, it must be accompanied by the same expression at A with the opposite sign, so that the whole vanishes at x = 0. In modern terms this is the boundary term [δy (∂Z/∂y' − d/dx ∂Z/∂y'' + ...)] taken from A to M. On the next page, these terms vanish when all comparison curves pass through A and M. Euler then handles free endpoints and an endpoint displaced along the curve (transversality-type terms, Z·dx).
errors: Logical gap: vanishing of the interior part (stationarity) is presented as implying that ∫Z dx 'vel maximum vel minimum obtinet valorem'. The Euler–Poisson equation is only necessary; no second-variation or sufficiency discussion is given. This is standard for the period.

The 'second part' shown is only the δy-component of the boundary term. For higher-order Z the full boundary term also contains δy′(Q − R′ + ...), δy″(R − ...), and so on. These presumably appear as further parts of the §14 solution not discussed on this page.
Printing slips in the displayed formulae: the last term of the first formula is printed with denominator dx³ (should be dx⁴). Some exponent superscripts are ill-formed (d^s S for d³S).

ideas.what: Vanishing of the interior part of the first variation for arbitrary δy is equivalent to the differential equation N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − ... = 0; such curves give extreme values.
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Poisson (higher-order Euler–Lagrange) equation via the fundamental lemma
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Methodus inveniendi); in variational form Lagrange (1760s) and Euler (E296, E420)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744); E296 Elementa calculi variationum (1766); E420

ideas.what: Boundary term δy·(P − Q′ + R″ − ...) evaluated as [ ]_A^M; it vanishes for fixed endpoints.
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms of the first variation / natural boundary conditions

ideas.what: Interpretation of the variation as a family y(x,t), with δy = dt·∂y/∂t as the small segment Yυ.
ideas.where_published: E420 and Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard expository page deriving the Euler–Poisson equation and fixed-endpoint boundary terms, which are well documented in the history of the calculus of variations.
transcription_corrections: In the first displayed formula the image shows the denominator of the S-term printed as dx³ (a misprint for dx⁴). The transcription silently gives dx⁴ and drops the trailing sign before 'etc.'
Second formula: the image reads 'd^s S / dx^3' (misprinted exponent for d³S) and ends '+ etc.'
Marginal note 'Explicatio partis secundae in variatione' sits beside §39.
